addressed_problems.content: The paper demonstrates that pruning improves certified robustness for ReLU-based neural networks under complete verification using the Branch-and-Bound framework, but all experiments are limited to relatively small convolutional models (e.g., a 7-layer network with about 200K parameters) that fit within a single 24GB GPU. Complete verification of larger architectures commonly used in practice triggers out-of-memory errors or exceeds the 300-second per-sample time limit. Consequently, it remains unresolved how the observed benefits of pruning—including verified-accuracy gains, reductions in verification time and GPU memory consumption, and the existence of certified lottery tickets—scale to substantially larger networks, deeper architectures, or models with different layer types, as the computational constraints of complete verification currently preclude such evaluation.

The paper identifies that pruning reduces neuron instability (measured by the fraction of ReLU neurons whose pre-activation bounds cross zero), which tightens verification bounds and improves certified accuracy. However, if too many neurons become stable, the network approaches a linear function, degrading standard accuracy. This creates a fundamental trade-off between stability and expressiveness. Designing principled methods to automatically select sparsity levels or stability-regularization strengths (e.g., the coefficient of NRSLoss) that maximize verified accuracy without unacceptable standard-accuracy loss remains unresolved. Current practice relies on empirical grid search, and no theoretical guidance exists for optimally balancing these competing objectives.

The paper evaluates pruning effects under two training regimes (auto-LiRPA certified training and FGSM+GradAlign adversarial training) and one complete verifier (Beta-CROWN), with a limited comparison to FastIBP certified training. A broader theoretical and empirical characterization of pruning's effects across other certified-training algorithms (e.g., other IBP variants, convex relaxation-based training), other complete verifiers (e.g., MIP-based, SMT-based), different model families (e.g., residual networks, transformers), and larger perturbation regimes (e.g., L2-norm, larger epsilon) remains open. Without such characterization, the generality of the conclusion that pruning generally improves certified robustness is uncertain, and the conditions under which pruning may hurt certified robustness are unknown.

The paper observes the existence of certified lottery tickets—sparse subnetworks that match both the standard and certified accuracies of the original dense model—across various pruning methods and datasets under certified training. However, the conditions under which such tickets exist (e.g., necessary sparsity levels, architectural properties, training hyperparameters) are not theoretically characterized. There are no existence proofs, bounds relating sparsity to certification preservation, or efficient algorithms to discover certified lottery tickets at scale without exhaustive iterative pruning. Developing such theoretical foundations and scalable discovery methods remains an open problem.

The paper proposes NRSLoss, a stability regularizer that normalizes the pre-activation bounds by the batch-normalization channel weight gamma and stops gradients from backpropagating to gamma. The NRSLoss weight is set empirically to 0.01, and the gradient-stopping design is motivated by training stability. Formal guidance for selecting the NRSLoss coefficient, understanding the sensitivity of certified accuracy to this hyperparameter, and proving the benefits of the gamma normalization and gradient-stopping are unresolved. Moreover, potential alternative BN-aware stability regularizers that are theoretically justified and robust to hyperparameter choices remain to be explored.

Contemporary certification of adversarial robustness for non-linear ReLU neural networks requires computing tight output bounds (so-called "complete verification") over an input domain. Prior to this work, complete verification remained computationally intractable in practice for all but small networks because (1) ReLU non-linearities force verifiers to either adopt loose linear relaxations (which produce overly loose bounds) or to branch on unstable ReLU units to obtain exact bounds, and tightening linear relaxations provably requires exponentially many constraints; and (2) Branch-and-Bound (BaB) style complete verifiers must explore an exponentially large number of ReLU sub-domains (branches) to obtain tight ground-truth bounds, so limited verification time yields loose certified bounds. At the same time, neural networks are heavily over-parameterized and various pruning techniques are widely used to reduce model size and computation, and some prior works reported that pruning can improve empirical (adversarial) robustness; however, before this work there was no systematic account of whether, why, or how pruning affects complete certified robustness (the verifier's estimated bound tightness and the model's ground-truth certifiable outputs). This gap matters because loose verifier bounds or intractable verification costs prevent reliable certification on realistic models, and there is no principled method to trade off network expressiveness (standard accuracy) against neuron stability (which governs branching and linear-relaxation looseness) to improve verifiability without destroying performance. Therefore a focused study was needed to (a) determine whether pruning generally helps complete verification certified robustness, (b) identify the mechanisms (e.g., reduction of neuron instability, fewer linear-relaxations, smaller weight matrices) by which pruning may alter verifier tightness and speed, and (c) design pruning objectives specifically targeted at the neuron-instability and BatchNorm interactions that impede certification.

nodes.content: In the context of complete verification of ReLU networks (the task of producing exact or tight output bounds for each input perturbation region), the central obstacle is verifier looseness and computational cost: LiRPA-style linear relaxations over unstable ReLU neurons are empirically and theoretically loose, and BaB-style complete verifiers require branching on unstable neurons which explodes the number of sub-domains explored. Prior to this conclusion, pruning was known to reduce parameter count or empirical adversarial vulnerability, but it was unclear whether pruning would systematically tighten verifier bounds or merely change empirical attack susceptibility. Because tight verified accuracy requires both a network whose true (ground-truth) outputs are robust and a verifier that can compute tight bounds within a time budget, confirming that standard pruning pipelines can produce subnetworks that improve the measurable (verified) robustness addresses a key practical barrier to applying complete verification: it suggests a simple model-reduction pathway that can both reduce verification cost and increase the fraction of inputs that verifiers can certify, without requiring fundamentally new verification algorithms.

Prior pruning and stability-regularization attempts (e.g., RS Loss) aimed to reduce unstable ReLU neurons but did not account for the scaling and optimization interactions introduced by Batch-Normalization layers. RS Loss operates on post-BN pre-activation bounds and therefore can inadvertently push gradients into BN scale parameters $\gamma$, restricting the effective optimization space and harming normal training convergence of pruned subnetworks. In certified verification, neuron instability (bound intervals straddling zero) increases the number of linear relaxations and BaB branches required, so a practical regularizer must both penalize neuron instability and avoid degrading BN-based training dynamics. NRSLoss directly regularizes the pre-BN bounds (achieved by dividing by $\gamma$ in the instability term), thereby penalizing neurons that are both unstable and of low channel importance, while blocking gradients into $\gamma$ to prevent BN-mediated optimization collapse. Before NRSLoss, there was no simple, BN-aware stability regularizer tailored for pruning that preserves training stability and explicitly targets the causes of verification looseness.

The central obstacle for practical complete verification is that linear-relaxation over unstable ReLU neurons is intrinsically loose and BaB branching to remove looseness is exponentially costly. Before this work there was no systematic empirical link demonstrated between standard pruning practices and the internal verification primitives (linear-relaxation looseness, count of unstable neurons, and number of sub-domain splits). Verifiers produce looser bounds and spend excessive time on models with many unstable neurons; therefore a mechanism that reduces unstable neurons and shrinks propagated interval radii is precisely what is needed to (i) improve bound tightness delivered within realistic timeouts and (ii) reduce verification resource consumption. Providing both the conceptual linkage (why pruning affects $|\mathbf{W}| r$ terms and branching load) and empirical evidence clarifies how model compression can be leveraged as a verification acceleration and tightening tool.

The lottery ticket hypothesis previously addressed matching dense-model test accuracy with sparse subnetworks, but it was unknown whether such "winning tickets" could also preserve or match the stricter criterion of complete-verification certified robustness (verified accuracy). Without evidence of certified lottery tickets, pruning could be dismissed as incompatible with certification because pruning might reduce model expressiveness in ways that systematically harm certifiability. Demonstrating certified lottery tickets shows that model compression can preserve the combination of expressiveness (standard accuracy) and verifiability (verified accuracy), thereby enabling reduced-size models that remain amenable to complete verification. This resolves the prior uncertainty about whether pruning can simultaneously preserve standard and certified performance.

Prior to these experiments there was no reported set of end-to-end complete-verification benchmarks demonstrating how much verified accuracy and verification resource usage can be improved by practical pruning schemes and stability-aware regularization. Verifiers and pruning methods were developed largely independently, so practitioners lacked quantitative expectations for gains achievable by pruning under complete verification. Providing measured percentage-point improvements on standard datasets and training regimes fills that gap and supplies concrete, reproducible targets for future method development and for practitioners deciding whether to prune models that must be certified.

Pruning a trained ReLU feed-forward convolutional network (using either unstructured or structured pruning paradigms, applied with iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) or other common criteria) produces subnetworks whose verified accuracy under complete verification (Beta-CROWN, a Branch-and-Bound-based complete verifier) is generally higher than the verified accuracy of the dense model. Verified accuracy is defined as the fraction of test samples for which the verifier establishes that the lower bound on the model score for the correct label exceeds the upper bound for every incorrect label under the considered input perturbation region (e.g., an L-infinity norm ball of radius epsilon). Empirically, on the FashionMNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10 datasets, under adversarial training with Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) with Gradient Alignment (GradAlign) and under certified training with Automatic Linear Relaxation based Perturbation Analysis (auto-LiRPA) / CROWN-IBP, representative pruning methods (IMP, SNIP, TaylorPruning, HYDRA, Network Slimming, StructLTH) yield consistent increases in verified accuracy relative to the dense baseline. Specifically, under certified training on CIFAR10, existing pruning methods improve verified accuracy by 1.6–7.1 percentage points; on FashionMNIST by 2.5–5.2 percentage points; on SVHN by 3.3–6.3 percentage points. Under adversarial training, improvements on CIFAR10 reach up to 24.5 percentage points (Network Slimming), on FashionMNIST from 21.0 to 40.0 percentage points, and on SVHN from 23.2 to 39.5 percentage points.

metadata.narrative: Premises P1 (single architecture), P2 (best-sparsity selection bias), and P3 (single verifier) each threaten the claim that pruning generally improves complete-verification certified robustness by limiting the evidential basis. P2 and P3 are the most load-bearing: selection bias and verifier-specificity could each invalidate the "generally" qualifier if true. However, highlights H1 (cross-dataset, cross-training consistency), H2 (multiple methods all improve), and H3 (improvement at larger perturbation) partially offset these risks by demonstrating a robust, widespread pattern across many settings within the tested scope. The conclusion is credible but its generality is scoped to feed-forward ReLU convnets similar to the tested architecture, evaluated with Beta-CROWN, with the reported improvements representing upper-bound rather than expected gains across sparsities.

nodes.title: Pruning generally improves complete-verification certified robustness of ReLU networks

nodes.content:
A stability-aware pruning regularizer, Normalized RS Loss (NRSLoss), is defined for a ReLU neuron with pre-activation bound interval $[\mathbf{l}_j, \mathbf{u}_j]$ and corresponding batch normalization (BN) channel weight $\gamma$ as:
      $$l_j^{\mathrm{nrs}} = -\tanh\!\Bigl(1 + \frac{\mathbf{l}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j}{\gamma^{2}}\Bigr),$$
      where $\mathbf{l}_j$ and $\mathbf{u}_j$ are the lower and upper pre-activation bounds for that neuron with respect to the input perturbation region, and $\gamma$ is the BN scaling parameter for the channel feeding the neuron. During training, NRSLoss is added to the primary loss with a coefficient of 0.01, and gradients from NRSLoss are stopped from flowing into $\gamma$ (stop-gradient to $\gamma$). Combining iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) with NRSLoss training (denoted IMP+NRSLoss) yields subnetworks that reduce network instability and achieve higher verified accuracy than the same pruning schedule without NRSLoss. The operational procedure is: train with the combined loss (primary loss + 0.01 * NRSLoss), compute neuron pre-activation bounds using Automatic Linear Relaxation based Perturbation Analysis (auto-LiRPA) during training, perform iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding, and repeat.

metadata.narrative: Premise P4 (hyperparameter sensitivity) is a refinement risk: if the NRSLoss weight or gradient-blocking choice is not robust, the method's effectiveness could degrade, but the qualitative benefit over RSLoss is still supported by highlight H5's direct ablation. Highlight H4 provides a theoretical grounding that makes the design principled rather than purely empirical. The combined weight of H4 and H5 insulates the conclusion from P4's concern: even if the specific hyperparameters are not optimal, the design logic is sound and the ablation demonstrates a real advantage. The conclusion that NRSLoss is an effective stability-aware pruning regularizer is well-supported.

nodes.title: Normalized RS Loss (NRSLoss): a stability-aware pruning regularizer and an effective pruning scheme (IMP+NRSLoss)

nodes.content: Pruning reduces the verifier's estimated bound looseness through two complementary mechanisms: (a) reducing weight-matrix magnitude and parameter count (e.g., in interval bound propagation (IBP), the propagated uncertainty term involves $|\mathbf{W}|$, which directly shrinks propagated interval radii); and (b) reducing the number and severity of unstable ReLU neurons (neurons whose pre-activation interval crosses zero), which reduces the number of neurons that must be linearly relaxed or explicitly branched by the Branch-and-Bound (BaB) algorithm. Together, these effects tighten the verifier's estimated bounds and lower verification time under a fixed timeout. Empirically, under FGSM+GradAlign adversarial training on CIFAR10, iterative pruning decreases the ratio of unstable ReLU neurons as sparsity increases (the ratio decreases with each pruning iteration). Structured pruning (Network Slimming) reduces average verification time (e.g., for models trained with auto-LiRPA, three pruning iterations with approximately 30% channel sparsity increase reduce verification time by about 50%; for models trained with FGSM, reduction is 60–80%) and reduces peak GPU memory consumption, while improving verified accuracy (e.g., on CIFAR10 under auto-LiRPA training, Network Slimming improves verified accuracy from 43.0% to 47.5% at a remain ratio of 0.79).

metadata.narrative: Premise P7 is a show-stopper for the causal claim that pruning tightens bounds specifically through reduced linear-relaxation looseness and sub-domain splits: the paper does not directly measure these intermediate quantities, and verification time reduction could be driven by the parameter-count mechanism alone (formally derived in H6). Premise P8 adds that the unstable-neuron reduction (H7) is shown only under FGSM, not under the certified training regime where the mechanism is claimed to operate. H6 provides rigorous support for the parameter-count tightening channel, and H7 provides direct evidence for the neuron-stability channel under FGSM, but under certified training the neuron-stability mechanism remains unconfirmed. The conclusion is therefore partially supported: the parameter-count tightening is firm, but the neuron-stability contribution to bound tightening under certified training is inferred rather than demonstrated.

nodes.title: Mechanism: pruning tightens verifier bounds by reducing linear-relaxation looseness and the need for sub-domain splits via decreased neuron instability

nodes.content: For the 7-layer ReLU convolutional architecture (three ConvBlock units with convolution-kernel sizes 3 or 4 and strides 1 or 2, followed by two fully-connected layers with 2048 and 100 units, using batch normalization after each convolution) trained with adversarial (Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) with Gradient Alignment (GradAlign)) or certified (Automatic Linear Relaxation based Perturbation Analysis (auto-LiRPA) / CROWN-IBP) training on FashionMNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10 datasets, there exist sparse subnetworks (found by iterative pruning procedures such as iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) or IMP+NRSLoss, and also other pruning methods) that match the original dense model in both standard accuracy and verified (complete-verification) accuracy. These subnetworks are termed "certified lottery tickets". Many pruning trajectories contain sparsities at which the pruned subnetwork's standard and verified accuracies are comparable to the dense baseline, and in several cases these subnetworks outperform the dense model on verified accuracy.

metadata.narrative: Premise P9 (no statistical test for matching) means the claim that subnetworks "match" dense model performance is asserted without rigorous uncertainty quantification. However, highlights H8 and H9 provide strong consistency evidence: the phenomenon appears across nine pruning methods, three datasets, two perturbation scales, and across multiple sparsity levels. The existence claim is credible even without a formal hypothesis test because the pattern is recurrent and systematic, reducing the likelihood that the reported matches are due to chance or selection. The conclusion is moderately supported; a statistical test would strengthen the "matching" characterization from plausible to rigorously established.

nodes.title: Existence of certified lottery tickets

nodes.content: On CIFAR10 using the 7-layer convolutional network under certified training with Automatic Linear Relaxation based Perturbation Analysis (auto-LiRPA) and perturbation radius $\epsilon = 2/255$, the IMP+NRSLoss pruning scheme increases verified accuracy by 8.2 percentage points (from 43.0% to 51.2%) and standard accuracy by 8.1 percentage points (from 54.1% to 62.2%) relative to the dense baseline at the best sparsity (remain ratio 0.21). Under adversarial training with Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) with Gradient Alignment (GradAlign) on CIFAR10, Network Slimming increases verified accuracy by 24.5 percentage points (from 1.5% to 26.0%) at remain ratio 0.35. On FashionMNIST under certified training, verified accuracy improvements range from 2.5 to 5.2 percentage points; under adversarial training, improvements range from 21.0 to 40.0 percentage points. On SVHN under certified training, verified accuracy improvements range from 3.3 to 6.3 percentage points; under adversarial training, improvements range from 23.2 to 39.5 percentage points. These numerical improvements are experimentally observed and result from the application of pruning and the NRSLoss treatment.

metadata.narrative: Premises P12 (best-sparsity selection) and P13 (small test set) introduce upward bias and variance into the reported quantitative improvements. P12 is particularly load-bearing because the reported gains (e.g., 8.2%, 24.5%) are maxima over sparsities, not expected values. Highlights H10 and H11 provide comprehensive reporting and cross-validation (FastIBP), which mitigate the bias somewhat by showing consistent patterns across methods and training regimes. The direction and qualitative magnitude of improvement are credible, but the specific percentage points likely overstate the typical gain a practitioner would obtain without multiple sparsity trials and selection.

nodes.title: Quantitative empirical improvements on CIFAR10 and other benchmarks

nodes.content: The complete-verification experiments are conducted on a single 7-layer feed-forward convolutional architecture: three ConvBlock units with convolution-kernel sizes 3 or 4 and strides 1 or 2, followed by two fully-connected layers with 2048 and 100 units, using ReLU activations and batch normalization after each convolution. No tests are conducted on other neural network architectures such as ResNets, VGG-style networks, or deeper networks that would exceed GPU memory for complete verification. Table III

metadata.failure_mode: If the architecture is not representative of other common model families (e.g., ResNets, VGG-style, or transformer-based), then the conclusion that pruning "generally improves" complete-verification certified robustness would be unsupported for those architectures. The claim of generality collapses, and the conclusion would only be valid for the specific 7-layer convnet studied. The paper's title and abstract imply broader applicability, so this failure would significantly narrow the conclusion's scope.
metadata.weakness_reason: The conclusion claims that pruning "generally improves complete-verification certified robustness", but the evidence base is a single architecture. Different architectures have different width-depth tradeoffs, different patterns of neuron instability, and different LiRPA bound-propagation characteristics. Without testing on at least one distinct family, the generality cannot be inferred; the result could be an artifact of the specific architecture's over-parameterization pattern.

nodes.title: Single architecture tested

nodes.content: For each pruning method, the reported verified accuracy is the maximum across the sparsity levels produced by iterative pruning (e.g., 16 iterations with a pruning rate of 0.2, producing remain ratios from 1.0 down to 0.03). The dense baseline is evaluated only at remain ratio 1.0. The average verified accuracy across sparsities and the distribution of improvements are not reported.

metadata.failure_mode: If the selection bias is positive, the claim that pruning "generally improves" certified accuracy is overstated. For a given method, the median or worst-case sparsity might show no improvement or even degradation, contradicting the "generally" qualifier. The quantitative improvements reported (e.g., 8.2% on CIFAR10) would be unrepresentative of typical performance.
metadata.weakness_reason: Selecting the best-performing sparsity per method introduces an optimistic bias in the comparison because the dense model is not similarly allowed to choose among multiple sparsities. Without accounting for this selection, the reported improvement is an upper bound on what a practitioner could expect by naively applying the method.

nodes.title: Best-sparsity selection bias

nodes.content: The main verified accuracy results are obtained using Beta-CROWN, a Branch-and-Bound (BaB) based complete verifier. The pruned subnetworks are not evaluated using other complete verifiers such as mixed integer programming (MIP)-based solvers or alternative BaB implementations like Fast-and-Complete without Beta-CROWN-specific optimizations.

metadata.failure_mode: If the improvements are specific to Beta-CROWN, then the conclusion that pruning improves "complete-verification certified robustness" would be misleading. The conclusion would need to be scoped to Beta-CROWN, and the general claim of improved certified robustness would be unsupported. The paper's broader message about pruning's benefits for certification would be weakened.
metadata.weakness_reason: Complete verifiers differ in their branching strategy, bounding functions, and reliance on linear relaxations. Beta-CROWN's per-neuron split constraints and optimizable Lagrange functions may interact differently with sparse networks than other verifiers. Without cross-verifier validation, it is unknown whether the improvements in verified accuracy are specific to Beta-CROWN or hold across complete verification frameworks.

nodes.title: Single verifier used

nodes.content: The Normalized RS Loss (NRSLoss) regularizer, defined as $l_j^{\mathrm{nrs}} = -\tanh(1 + (\mathbf{l}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j) / \gamma^2)$, is used with a weight of 0.01 added to the primary loss, and gradients to the batch normalization channel weight $\gamma$ are stopped. No sensitivity analysis is provided for the weight coefficient or for the gradient-blocking design choice; these hyperparameters are set empirically based on a single configuration.

metadata.failure_mode: If the NRSLoss weight or the gradient-blocking design is not robust (i.e., small changes cause significant performance degradation), the conclusion that NRSLoss is an effective pruning regularizer would be weakened. The method would be seen as brittle and its practical value diminished. The ablation advantage over RSLoss (H5) would be less general.
metadata.weakness_reason: Any regularizer's effectiveness can be sensitive to its coefficient and interaction with optimization. The choice to stop gradients to gamma is a non-standard intervention that could affect training dynamics in ways not yet understood. Without a sensitivity sweep across a range of weights or an ablation of the gradient-blocking choice, the claimed effectiveness may be contingent on this specific hyperparameter configuration.

nodes.title: NRSLoss hyperparameters unswept

nodes.content: It is claimed that pruning tightens verifier bounds by reducing the number of linear relaxations and Branch-and-Bound (BaB) sub-domain splits due to decreased neuron instability. However, the number of linear relaxations performed, the number of sub-domains explored by BaB, and the bound tightness gap (difference between verifier output and ground-truth bound) before versus after pruning are not directly measured. Instead, these reductions are inferred from (a) a decrease in the ratio of unstable ReLU neurons (pre-activation bounds crossing zero) and (b) a decrease in verification time and GPU memory consumption.

metadata.failure_mode: If verification time reduction is primarily due to reduced weight matrix size (as formally derived in H6) rather than to reduced linear-relaxation looseness or sub-domain splits, then the proposed mechanism for bound tightening through neuron stability is not the dominant factor and may even be absent. The conclusion's explanatory claim (that pruning tightens bounds by reducing linear relaxations and splits) would be unsupported, leaving only the parameter-count mechanism as confirmed.
metadata.weakness_reason: A decrease in verification time can be explained by the parameter-count mechanism alone (reduced matrix multiplications) without any improvement in linear-relaxation tightness or sub-domain splits. The neuron-instability decrease (shown only under FGSM) may contribute but is not directly linked to BaB branching statistics. Without direct measurements of the claimed intermediate variables, the causal chain remains correlational rather than established.

nodes.title: Causal mechanism not directly measured

nodes.content: Under FGSM+GradAlign adversarial training on CIFAR10, the ratio of unstable ReLU neurons decreases with pruning sparsity (as observed in experimental data, the ratio decreases monotonically with pruning iterations). Under auto-LiRPA certified training, no analogous data on unstable neuron ratios are presented. Thus, the claim that pruning reduces neuron instability under certified training is supported only by indirect evidence (verified accuracy improvements) rather than by direct measurement of the claimed intermediate variable.

metadata.failure_mode: If pruning under certified training does not cause a comparable reduction in neuron instability, then the claimed mechanism (decreased instability leading to tighter bounds) does not apply to the certified training setting, which is the primary setting where pruning shows large verified accuracy improvements. The conclusion's mechanism would then be validated only for adversarial training, limiting its scope.
metadata.weakness_reason: Certified training (auto-LiRPA) explicitly encourages stable neurons through CROWN-IBP bound computation, so the effect of pruning on instability may be weaker or qualitatively different than under FGSM. Without direct evidence, the mechanism under the certified training regime—where the most substantial verified accuracy gains are reported—remains speculative.

nodes.title: Unstable neuron reduction shown only under FGSM

nodes.content: It is stated that sparse subnetworks found by pruning under certified training 'match' the dense model in both standard accuracy and verified accuracy. However, no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or statistical significance are reported for the observed differences. The matching claim is based on point estimates from a limited number of seeds: 5 seeds for auto-LiRPA on CIFAR10 (results averaged) and a single seed for other settings.

metadata.failure_mode: If a formal test would reveal that the subnetworks' accuracies are not statistically indistinguishable from the dense model (e.g., due to high variance or small but consistent deficits in some metrics), then the existence of certified lottery tickets that "match" both accuracies would not be supported. The phenomenon would be demoted to "subnetworks that are within a few percentage points," which is weaker than the claimed equivalence.
metadata.weakness_reason: Without uncertainty quantification, it is impossible to distinguish between true equal performance and noise. Given the small verification test set (200 images) and the variance in training, small point differences could easily be within sampling or training noise. The claim of "matching" is therefore imprecise and potentially overstated.

nodes.title: No statistical test for matching

nodes.content: On CIFAR10 under auto-LiRPA certified training, IMP+NRSLoss increases verified accuracy by 8.2 percentage points over the dense baseline (from 43.0% to 51.2%). This improvement is the maximum across iterative pruning sparsities; the median or mean improvement across sparsities is not reported, nor are confidence intervals for the improvement.

metadata.failure_mode: If the true expected improvement (e.g., mean across sparsities or at a typical sparsity) is substantially smaller than the reported maximum, then the quantitative claims (8.2%, 24.5%) misrepresent the practical benefit of pruning. The conclusion that pruning yields large verified accuracy gains would be quantitatively overstated.
metadata.weakness_reason: Reporting only the maximum improvement across sparsities creates an optimistic bias. The same procedure that selects the best sparsity for pruning also selects the best-reported gain, which is not the expected gain from a single application of the method. The paper does not correct for this multiplicity.

nodes.title: Best-sparsity selection for quantitative numbers

nodes.content: All verified accuracy estimates are computed on a small subset of the test set: 200 images for FashionMNIST and SVHN, and the first 200 images of the ERAN test set for CIFAR10 (which contains 1000 images in total). Bootstrap confidence intervals or standard errors for these estimates are not reported.

metadata.failure_mode: If the true verified accuracy on the full test set differs by several percentage points from the reported estimates, the specific quantitative improvements (e.g., 8.2% instead of a true 5% or 10%) would be inaccurate. The conclusion's quantitative precision is undermined, though the qualitative direction remains plausible.
metadata.weakness_reason: A sample of 200 images yields a standard error of roughly sqrt(p*(1-p)/200) for a binary accuracy metric, which is about 3.5 percentage points at p=50% and 2.1 points at p=90%. Differences of a few percentage points thus have substantial uncertainty. Without error bars, the reported improvements cannot be assessed for statistical reliability.

nodes.title: Small verification test set

nodes.content: On three datasets (FashionMNIST with epsilon=0.1, SVHN with epsilon=2/255, CIFAR10 with epsilon=2/255) and under two training methods (FGSM adversarial training and auto-LiRPA certified training), all eight tested pruning methods (IMP, SNIP, TP, HYDRA, HYDRA+NRSLoss, IMP+RSLoss, IMP+NRSLoss, StructLTH, Slim) improved verified accuracy over the dense baseline in every evaluated condition.

metadata.credit: This cross-dataset and cross-training consistency insulates the conclusion from being dismissed as an artifact of a single benchmark or training regimen. Without this breadth, the claim of generality would rest on one or two combinations, which could be due to idiosyncratic factors. The unbroken improvement across 3 datasets × 2 training methods × multiple methods provides strong multiplicative evidence that the phenomenon is robust.

nodes.title: Cross-dataset and cross-training improvement consistency

nodes.content: The paper tests six distinct off-the-shelf pruning methods from different families: magnitude-based (IMP), gradient-sensitivity-based (SNIP, TaylorPruning), robustness-loss-based (HYDRA), and structured methods (StructLTH, Network Slimming). All methods increase verified accuracy over the dense baseline on CIFAR10 under auto-LiRPA (range 1.6-7.1% improvement) and under FGSM (range 12.5-24.5%).

metadata.credit: The plurality of methods rules out the alternative that a single pruning algorithm's peculiarity causes the improvement. Without this diversity, the conclusion could be questioned as method-specific. The fact that every tested method, regardless of its criterion, improves verified accuracy strongly suggests that the pruning operation itself—reducing parameters—is the driving factor, not any particular selection rule.

nodes.title: Multiple pruning methods all improve

nodes.content: On CIFAR10 with a four-times-larger perturbation epsilon=8/255, IMP and IMP+NRSLoss produce subnetworks with higher verified accuracy (29.8% and 31.5% respectively) compared to the dense baseline (29.3%) under auto-LiRPA certified training.

metadata.credit: The perturbation radius is four times larger (8/255 vs 2/255). If pruning only helped at small perturbations (where bounds are already tight), the conclusion would have limited practical significance. Showing improvement at a larger perturbation extends the regime of validity and suggests the mechanism (reduced parameter count and unstable neurons) scales with input size.

nodes.title: Improvement at larger perturbation

nodes.content: NRSLoss is defined as l_j^{nrs} = -tanh(1 + (l_j * u_j) / gamma^2), where [l_j, u_j] are the pre-activation bounds of ReLU neuron j and gamma is the BN channel weight. The loss penalizes instability (negative l_j * u_j) normalized by gamma^2, making the penalty high only when instability is large relative to the channel importance scale gamma. Gradients from NRSLoss are blocked from flowing to gamma to avoid distorting BN training. The loss landscape (Figure 2 in paper) shows that NRSLoss naturally suppresses regularization on important (large-gamma) neurons even when they are moderately unstable.

metadata.credit: The theoretical grounding demonstrates that NRSLoss is not an ad-hoc heuristic but targets the specific interaction between neuron instability and BN channel importance that hampers certified robustness. Without this motivation, the regularizer's design would appear arbitrary, and the conclusion that NRSLoss is effective would be purely empirical and could be questioned if the empirical setting changed. The credit is that the conclusion's mechanism is principled, increasing confidence that NRSLoss will transfer to related settings.

nodes.title: Theoretical grounding of NRSLoss

nodes.content: On CIFAR10 under auto-LiRPA certified training (epsilon=2/255), IMP+NRSLoss achieves verified accuracy 51.2% (dense 43.0%, improvement +8.2%) and standard accuracy 62.2% (dense 54.1%, improvement +8.1%). IMP+RSLoss achieves verified accuracy 46.3% (improvement +3.3%) and standard accuracy 58.6% (improvement +4.5%). Both use the same IMP pruning schedule and differ only in whether the regularizer pre-divides by gamma and stops gradients to gamma.

metadata.credit: This direct controlled comparison isolates the effect of normalizing the stability penalty by BN channel gamma and blocking gradients to gamma. Without this ablation, the improvement over plain IMP might be attributed to the stability penalty in general, not specifically to the BN-aware design. The comparison shows that the BN-aware modification is responsible for the additional gain, strongly supporting the claim that NRSLoss's design choices are effective.

nodes.title: Ablation IMP+NRSLoss beats IMP+RSLoss

nodes.content: For a linear layer, Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) computes output bound radius as r_k = |W| r_{k-1}, where |W| is the elementwise absolute weight matrix and r_{k-1} is the input radius. Pruning makes W sparser, reducing the entries of |W| and thereby directly reducing r_k, tightening the propagated bounds at every linear layer.

metadata.credit: This provides a rigorous algebraic mechanism by which pruning tightens bounds, independent of neuron stability. Without this formal link, the claim that pruning tightens verifier bounds would be only intuitive. The formal derivation shows that even in the absence of neuron stability changes, pruning has a guaranteed bound-tightening effect, which is load-bearing for the conclusion that pruning improves verified accuracy.

nodes.title: Formal IBP bound-tightening derivation

nodes.content: Under FGSM adversarial training, the paper measures the ratio of unstable ReLU neurons (pre-activation bounds crossing zero) as a function of iterative pruning steps for IMP, SNIP, TP, and HYDRA on CIFAR10. For all four methods, the unstable neuron ratio monotonically decreases as sparsity increases, from approximately 0.5 at the dense model to below 0.1 at the highest sparsity levels.

metadata.credit: This direct measurement provides the key link between pruning and the neuron-stability mechanism. Without it, the mechanism would be theoretical speculation. The fact that multiple pruning methods all reduce instability supports the causal pathway from sparsity to reduced linear relaxations. The credit is that the mechanism's empirical support is not limited to one method, increasing confidence.

nodes.title: Empirical unstable neuron reduction

nodes.content: Under auto-LiRPA certified training on all three datasets (FashionMNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10), nine pruning methods (IMP, SNIP, TP, HYDRA, HYDRA+NRSLoss, IMP+RSLoss, IMP+NRSLoss, StructLTH, Slim) all produce at least one subnetwork whose standard accuracy and verified accuracy equal or exceed the dense model's. On CIFAR10 at epsilon=8/255, IMP and IMP+NRSLoss also produce such subnetworks.

metadata.credit: The phenomenon is observed across nine pruning methods and three datasets plus two perturbation scales. This breadth rules out the possibility that the observation is a fluke of a specific method or dataset. Without this consistency, the existence of certified lottery tickets would be suspect. The credit is that the existence claim is backed by multiple independent confirmations.

nodes.title: Certified tickets across pruning methods and datasets

nodes.content: For IMP and IMP+NRSLoss under auto-LiRPA on CIFAR10 (epsilon=2/255), Figure 6(a) shows that the verified accuracy exceeds the dense baseline at six out of seven evaluated iterative pruning steps (sparsities from 0.21 to 0.03 remain ratio), not just at the best sparsity.

metadata.credit: If the certified lottery ticket only occurred at one specific sparsity, it would be vulnerable to selection bias concerns. The pattern of sustained superior performance across multiple sparsities indicates that the phenomenon is intrinsic to the subnetworks at various sparsity levels, making it more credible that a lottery ticket exists and can be reliably found.

nodes.title: Certified tickets at multiple sparsities

nodes.content: Table I reports for each dataset (FashionMNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10), pruning method, and training regime (FGSM and auto-LiRPA) the remain ratio, standard accuracy (std), adversarial accuracy (adv, for FGSM only), verified accuracy (ver), and verification time in seconds (t). The dense baseline is included in each sub-table for direct comparison.

metadata.credit: The thoroughness of reporting enables reproducibility and cross-comparison. Without a detailed breakdown, the quantitative improvements would be opaque and difficult to verify. The table provides the concrete empirical support for all quantitative claims in conclusion 5.

nodes.title: Comprehensive measurement table

nodes.content: Under FastIBP certified training on CIFAR10 (epsilon=2/255), IMP+NRSLoss achieves verified accuracy 54.0% (dense 43.5%, improvement +10.5%), IMP achieves 53.0% (improvement +9.5%), HYDRA achieves 51.0% (improvement +7.5%), and other methods also show improvements. The dense baseline's verified accuracy under FastIBP is 43.5% (comparable to 43.0% under auto-LiRPA).

metadata.credit: This independent replication under a different certified training method with lower loss-fusion shows that the quantitative improvements are not an artifact of the auto-LiRPA training pipeline. Without this, the numbers could be dismissed as specific to auto-LiRPA's bound computation during training. The cross-validation strengthens the conclusion that pruning leads to real verified accuracy gains.

nodes.title: Validation with FastIBP certified training

steps.reasoning: Define "verified accuracy" for complete verification explicitly: verified accuracy is the fraction of test samples for which the verifier establishes that the lower bound on the model score for the correct label exceeds the upper bound for every incorrect label under the considered input perturbation region (i.e., the verifier certifies the model's prediction is invariant across the perturbation set for that sample).

State the experimental verification and evaluation setup that supports the general empirical claim: the authors evaluate pruning effects on certified robustness under complete verification using a GPU-parallelized Branch-and-Bound verifier (Beta-CROWN) and test on FashionMNIST, SVHN and CIFAR10 benchmark datasets using a 7-layer feed-forward convolutional neural network architecture; verification is executed on the first 200 test samples (or 1000 ERAN test images truncated to 200 for efficiency), with a per-sample timeout of 300 seconds, and Beta-CROWN is used to compute final verified accuracies reported in tables. These evaluation choices and verifier enable comparison of verified accuracy between dense and pruned models.
[35]
Fig. 5

List the pruning methods and training schemes empirically compared so the claim pertains to a broad set of methods: the authors test representative unstructured pruning methods (IMP, SNIP, TaylorPruning, HYDRA) and structured pruning methods (Network Slimming, StructLTH), as well as their proposed stability-aware method (IMP+NRSLoss), combined with both adversarial training (FGSM+GradAlign) and certified training (auto-LiRPA/CROWN-IBP); these methods therefore form the experimental basis for claiming that pruning generally improves certified robustness across paradigms.
[29]

Present the empirical aggregated results that support the generality claim: under the auto-LiRPA (certified-training) setting the authors report that existing pruning methods improve verified accuracies by approximately $2.5\text{--}5.2\%$ on FashionMNIST, $3.3\text{--}6.3\%$ on SVHN, and $1.6\text{--}7.1\%$ on CIFAR10 (these ranges are reported by the authors when summarizing their Table I and Table II results); under the FGSM+GradAlign (adversarial-training) setting the authors report much larger verified-accuracy increases in many cases (e.g., up to $24.5$ percentage points on CIFAR10 and larger gains on other datasets in the adversarial-training rows of the big experimental table). These numeric improvements are presented in the paper's experiment tables and described in the results text as consistent increases relative to dense baselines.
Table I
Table II

Cite illustrative single-case numeric evidence reported by the authors to make the general claim concrete: for CIFAR10 (the 7-layer convolutional model used in the paper) under certified-training (auto-LiRPA) with perturbation radius $\epsilon=2/255$, IMP (and other representative pruning schemes) produce verified-accuracy gains in the $1.6\text{--}7.1\%$ range compared to the dense baseline, and the proposed IMP+NRSLoss produces an $8.2$ percentage point verified-accuracy gain in the authors' reported experiments; under adversarial training (FGSM+GradAlign) some pruning methods yield verified-accuracy gains up to $24.5$ percentage points on CIFAR10. These explicit numeric comparisons are taken from the authors' tabulated results.
Table II

Report the qualitative support in verification curves and instability plots: the verified-accuracy versus iterative pruning-times curves (for example on CIFAR10 in the paper's plots) show that many pruning trajectories produce subnetworks with higher verified accuracy than the dense baseline at particular sparsities, and the authors' instability plots (ratio of unstable neurons versus pruning times) corroborate the mechanism by which pruning produces these verified-accuracy improvements (i.e., reduced instability leads to tighter bounds and higher verified accuracy).
Fig. 6
Fig. 4

Summarize the empirical scope and consistency: across datasets (FashionMNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10), across pruning paradigms (unstructured and structured), across pruning criteria (iterative magnitude-based IMP and other criteria), and across training regimes (adversarial FGSM+GradAlign and certified auto-LiRPA/CROWN-IBP), the representative pruning methods tested by the authors yield consistent increases in verified accuracy relative to the dense baseline in the authors' experiments; thus pruning generally improves complete-verification certified robustness in the settings and benchmarks the authors evaluated.

Conclude (as the authors do): combining the experimental evidence above with the mechanism that pruning tightens verifier bounds via reduced weight magnitudes and reduced neuron instability (established earlier), the paper's empirical claim that pruning generally improves complete-verification certified robustness for ReLU feed-forward convolutional networks (both unstructured and structured paradigms) is supported by the presented experiments and analyses.

Start from the upstream result: pruning tightens verifier-estimated bounds by reducing weight magnitudes / parameter counts and by reducing the number/severity of unstable ReLU neurons (the mechanism established previously). Treat that mechanism as known for the subsequent motivation of a stability-aware regularizer that explicitly targets neuron instability during training.

Introduce the RS Loss stability regularizer and its motivation: define the RS Loss for a neuron as $l_{j}^{rs}=-\tanh\!\bigl(1+\mathbf{l}_{j}\cdot\mathbf{u}_{j}\bigr)$ where $\mathbf{l}_{j}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{j}$ are the lower and upper pre-activation bounds of the neuron; state that $-\mathbf{l}_{j}\cdot\mathbf{u}_{j}$ measures instability (it is large when the interval straddles zero and is most extreme when $\mathbf{l}_{j}=-\mathbf{u}_{j}$ for fixed width), and the $\tanh$ wrapper gives a smooth loss suitable for gradient-based optimization. The RS Loss thus penalizes unstable neurons to reduce network instability.
[41]

Explain why RS Loss needs adaptation when Batch Normalization (BN) is present: define $\gamma$ as the BN scaling parameter (channel weight) for the channel feeding the ReLU neuron; note that BN scales pre-BN bounds by $\gamma$ and thus directly affects the magnitudes of $\mathbf{l}_{j}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{j}$, which can cause RS Loss gradients to flow into $\gamma$ and distort training—empirically this made RS Loss ineffective for deep networks with BN in the authors' experiments.
Fig. 2

Define the Normalized RS Loss (NRSLoss): for a ReLU neuron with pre-activation bounds $\mathbf{l}_j,\mathbf{u}_j$ and the BN channel weight $\gamma$, define
$$
l_{j}^{\mathrm{nrs}} \;=\; -\tanh\!\Bigl(1 + \frac{\mathbf{l}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j}{\gamma^{2}}\Bigr).
$$
Explain that dividing by $\gamma^{2}$ effectively computes RS Loss on the pre-BN bounds $\mathbf{l}_j/\gamma$ and $\mathbf{u}_j/\gamma$, disentangling the instability regularization from the BN scaling so BN can still be learned normally.

Specify training-time implementation details for NRSLoss: during training NRSLoss is added to the primary loss with an empirical coefficient (the authors use coefficient $0.01$), and gradients from NRSLoss are blocked from flowing into the BN scaling parameter $\gamma$ (i.e., stop-gradient to $\gamma$) to prevent NRSLoss from interfering with BN parameter learning. The bound computations used in NRSLoss during training are obtained from auto-LiRPA during certified training and from IBP during adversarial training, per the authors' training setups.
[42]
Fig. 2

Describe the combined pruning scheme IMP+NRSLoss (operational procedure): define IMP as Iterative Magnitude Pruning which iteratively prunes a fraction of smallest-magnitude weights and rewinds the remaining weights to earlier initialization states; the authors train the network with the combined loss (primary loss + $0.01\times$ NRSLoss), compute neuron pre-activation bounds using auto-LiRPA (during certified training), perform iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding (IMP), and repeat the train-prune-rewind iterations to obtain subnetworks. The authors denote this complete pipeline as IMP+NRSLoss.
[8]

Explain the intended effect of IMP+NRSLoss: because the model is trained with a weighted combination of the robustness/primary loss and NRSLoss, the magnitude of each trained individual weight reflects its saliency with respect to both robustness and neuron stability. Thus, pruning by smallest magnitude in this combined-trained model preferentially removes weights that are low-saliency for both robustness and stability, thereby producing subnetworks with reduced instability and improved verified accuracy relative to IMP without NRSLoss.

Present the empirical evidence the authors report that IMP+NRSLoss reduces instability and improves verified accuracy: (a) the network instability curves (the pre-activation instability metric defined as $\sum_{i}\sum_{j}-\mathbf{l}_{j}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_{j}^{(i)}$) show significantly lower instability for RS Loss and NRSLoss-based pruning compared to vanilla IMP, and instability decreases as sparsity increases; (b) verified-accuracy results in the tabulated experiments show IMP+NRSLoss achieving higher verified accuracy than the same pruning schedule without NRSLoss, e.g., on CIFAR10 with certified-training (auto-LiRPA) at perturbation radius $\epsilon=2/255$, IMP+NRSLoss increases verified accuracy by $8.2$ percentage points and standard accuracy by $8.1$ percentage points relative to the dense baseline at the reported pruning sparsity; these empirical items are reported in the authors' tables and figures.
Fig. 8
Table II

Note qualitative landscape evidence: the authors plot NRSLoss landscapes showing that NRSLoss penalizes neurons with high instability and low BN-channel importance ($\gamma$), illustrating the design intent that NRSLoss regularizes instability while avoiding over-regularizing important channels; this supports the observed empirical benefit in stability and verified accuracy for IMP+NRSLoss.
Fig. 2

Conclude (as the authors do): NRSLoss is a stability-aware pruning regularizer defined by $l_{j}^{\mathrm{nrs}}=-\tanh\!\bigl(1 + \frac{\mathbf{l}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j}{\gamma^{2}}\bigr)$ where $\mathbf{l}_j,\mathbf{u}_j$ are pre-activation bounds and $\gamma$ is the BN channel scale; training with NRSLoss (coefficient $0.01$) while blocking gradients to $\gamma$, and combining with iterative magnitude pruning and weight rewinding (IMP+NRSLoss), yields subnetworks with reduced neuron instability and higher verified accuracy than the same pruning schedule without NRSLoss, as supported by the authors' empirical instability plots and verified-accuracy tables.
[41]

Define the pre-activation bound interval of the $j$-th ReLU neuron at layer $i$ as $[\mathbf{l}_{j}^{(i)},\mathbf{u}_{j}^{(i)}]$, where $\mathbf{l}_{j}^{(i)}$ is the lower bound and $\mathbf{u}_{j}^{(i)}$ is the upper bound of the pre-activation value under the considered input perturbation region; a neuron is called "unstable" when $\mathbf{l}_{j}^{(i)}<0<\mathbf{u}_{j}^{(i)}$ (i.e., the interval crosses zero), and "stable" when $\mathbf{l}_{j}^{(i)}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{j}^{(i)}$ have the same sign. The distinction between stable and unstable ReLU neurons determines whether a ReLU can be treated as linear (stable) or requires linear relaxation / branching (unstable), which directly affects verifier bound tightness and branching needs. 
Fig. 3

Present the interval bound propagation (IBP) linear-layer propagation formulas used to illustrate how layer weights influence propagated interval radii: define $\bar{z}_{k-1}$ and $\underline{z}_{k-1}$ as the input upper and lower bounds to the linear layer, define $\mu_{k-1}=\tfrac{\bar{z}_{k-1}+\underline{z}_{k-1}}{2}$ as the midpoint, define $r_{k-1}=\tfrac{\bar{z}_{k-1}-\underline{z}_{k-1}}{2}$ as the radius, denote the linear-layer weight matrix as $\mathbf{W}$ and bias as $b$, and compute
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{k} &=\mathbf{W} \mu_{k-1}+b,\\
r_{k} &=|\mathbf{W}|\, r_{k-1},\\
\underline{z}_{k} &=\mu_{k}-r_{k},\\
\bar{z}_{k} &=\mu_{k}+r_{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$
From these expressions the difference between output upper and lower bound equals $2\,r_{k}=2\,|\mathbf{W}|\, r_{k-1}$, which shows that the elementwise magnitude of $\mathbf{W}$ ($|\mathbf{W}|$) directly scales the propagated interval radii.

Conclude from the IBP formulas that reducing weight magnitudes or removing parameters (making $\mathbf{W}$ sparser or smaller in magnitude) will reduce $|\mathbf{W}|\, r_{k-1}$ and thus shrink the propagated interval radius $r_{k}$, tightening the interval bounds at that layer and downstream; therefore pruning (which reduces weight magnitudes and parameter count) directly tightens propagated IBP-style interval bounds, reducing linear-relaxation looseness that arises from large propagated radii.

Explain the separate mechanism involving unstable ReLU neurons and Branch-and-Bound (BaB) style complete verification: define BaB as a divide-and-conquer verifier that recursively splits the input domain by branching on ReLU activations (i.e., choosing sub-domains corresponding to ReLU being active vs. inactive) and computes bounds on each sub-domain; because an unstable neuron (one with $\mathbf{l}<0<\mathbf{u}$) cannot be treated as purely linear without relaxation or branching, each unstable neuron either forces a linear relaxation (which loosens bounds) or an explicit branch (which multiplies sub-domains). The number of sub-domains grows exponentially in the number of branched unstable neurons, making BaB verification time extremely sensitive to the count and severity of unstable neurons. 
[4]

Combine the two mechanisms: pruning reduces weight magnitudes and parameter counts (mechanism A from the IBP formulas) which shrinks the propagated interval radii; pruning can also reduce the number and severity of unstable neurons (mechanism B), thereby reducing the number of neurons requiring linear relaxation or explicit branching in BaB; together these effects tighten verifier-estimated bounds and reduce the verifier's branching workload and verification time under a fixed per-sample timeout.
[28]

Record the empirical evidence the authors present for the instability-reduction mechanism: the authors plot the ratio of unstable neurons versus pruning times (i.e., increasing sparsity) and observe that the ratio of unstable neurons generally decreases as sparsity increases, demonstrating that iterative pruning decreases neuron instability in practice; this empirical curve is presented in the paper and used to support the claim that pruning reduces the number of unstable neurons.
Fig. 4

Record the empirical evidence the authors present for the verification-efficiency and bound-tightening consequences: the authors report that structured pruning reduces average verification time and peak GPU memory consumption (showing concrete reductions in verification runtime and memory at increasing channel sparsity), and they report improved verified accuracies for pruned models in tabulated results; these empirical observations together support that pruning both tightens verifier bounds and lowers verification resource usage in practice.
Fig. 7
Table II

Note supporting theoretical and empirical context cited by the authors about why linear relaxations are loose and why fewer unstable neurons matter: the linear-relaxation approximation for unstable ReLU neurons is known to be loose both empirically and theoretically, tightening such relaxations would generally require exponentially many linear constraints, and the BaB branching requirement is exponential in the worst case; these prior results contextualize why reducing relaxation looseness and branching needs via pruning can materially improve verifier-estimated bounds and runtime.
[16]
[33]

Conclude (as the authors do): pruning tightens verifier-estimated bounds via two complementary mechanisms (A) reducing weight-matrix magnitude and parameter count which directly shrinks propagated interval radii, and (B) reducing the number and severity of unstable ReLU neurons which reduces required linear relaxations and branching in BaB; together these effects tighten verifier bounds and lower verification time under fixed timeout, as supported by the IBP formulas, the BaB branching description, and the empirical figures/tables.

Define "certified lottery ticket": a sparse subnetwork obtained by pruning that can match the original dense model in both standard (unperturbed) accuracy and verified (complete-verification) accuracy; this extends the lottery ticket hypothesis notion of "winning tickets" to the certified-robustness setting.
[8]

Describe the pruning and evaluation procedure that produced candidate certified lottery tickets: the authors apply iterative pruning with weight rewinding (Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP) and other pruning methods to produce subnetworks at multiple sparsities, training each pruned subnetwork (rewinding weights as described) and then evaluating standard and verified accuracies with Beta-CROWN on the test samples; this per-sparsity evaluation yields the data used to judge whether a subnetwork matches the dense model in both metrics.
[8]

Present the empirical observation supporting existence: the authors report that for all pruning methods under certified training across the three datasets (FashionMNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10) they tested, there exist sparsities at which the pruned subnetworks' standard and verified accuracies are statistically indistinguishable from the dense baseline, and many pruning trajectories contain such sparsities; in several cases the pruned subnetworks even outperform the dense model on verified accuracy. The authors explicitly state this finding in the experiments section and present supporting tabular and curve data.
Fig. 6
Table I

Note the authors' additional empirical claims: the occurrence of such certified lottery tickets is robust across pruning methods (IMP and NRSLoss-based procedures are specifically highlighted), and the authors observe that certified lottery tickets appear in many sparsities (i.e., not only at a single precisely tuned sparsity), which the authors view as evidence that certified lottery tickets are a reproducible phenomenon in their experimental setting.
Fig. 10

Conclude (as the authors do): the experiments validate the existence of certified lottery tickets—sparse subnetworks found by iterative pruning procedures that can match both standard and complete-verification certified accuracies of the original dense models—across tested datasets and pruning methods.

Start from the upstream result that NRSLoss and IMP+NRSLoss produce subnetworks with reduced neuron instability and improved verified accuracy relative to IMP alone (treat conclusion 2 as established); use that result as contextual foundation for reporting the paper's concrete numeric experimental improvements.

State the CIFAR10 certified-training numeric result explicitly: define the setting as the 7-layer convolutional model under certified-training with auto-LiRPA at perturbation radius $\epsilon=2/255$, denote the dense baseline standard accuracy as $std_{dense}=54.1\%$ and verified accuracy as $ver_{dense}=43.0\%$ as reported by the authors, and denote the IMP+NRSLoss pruned model reported at the chosen pruning sparsity as having $std_{\text{IMP+NRSLoss}}=62.2\%$ and $ver_{\text{IMP+NRSLoss}}=51.2\%$; therefore IMP+NRSLoss increases verified accuracy by $51.2-43.0=8.2$ percentage points and standard accuracy by $62.2-54.1=8.1$ percentage points relative to the dense baseline at the reported pruning sparsity (these numbers are taken from the authors' table entries).
Table II

State the CIFAR10 adversarial-training numeric result explicitly: define the adversarial-training setting as FGSM+GradAlign, denote the dense baseline verified accuracy under FGSM for CIFAR10 as $ver_{dense}^{\text{FGSM}}=1.5\%$ (as reported), and cite the Network Slimming (Slim) or other pruning-method row that reports $ver_{\text{Slim}}=26.0\%$ with the annotation $(+24.5)$ in the authors' FGSM table, which indicates a verified-accuracy increase of $24.5$ percentage points versus the dense baseline; thus under adversarial training certain pruning methods increase verified accuracy by up to $24.5$ percentage points on CIFAR10 in the authors' experiments.
Table I

State comparable numeric summaries on FashionMNIST and SVHN as reported by the authors: for FashionMNIST the authors report certified-training verified-accuracy gains in the range approximately $2.5\text{--}6.3\%$ and adversarial-training verified-accuracy gains in the range $21.0\text{--}41.5\%$ on selected pruning setups (e.g., IMP+NRSLoss row reports ver $41.5\%$ with $(+40.0)$ under FGSM in the FashionMNIST table), and for SVHN the authors report similar improvements (e.g., IMP+NRSLoss shows ver increases of multiple percentage points under auto-LiRPA and large gains under FGSM), so the paper summarizes these datasets with the ranges stated above based on their tabulated experiment rows.
Table I

Clarify that these numerical gains are empirical and attributable to the pruning and NRSLoss treatments in the authors' experiments: the authors explicitly state that the reported percentage-point increases would not exist absent the pruning procedures and NRSLoss training applied in the experiments, and the tabulated comparisons contrast dense baselines with the pruned-method rows to substantiate these differences.
Table II

Conclude (as the authors do): concrete experimental measurements include the CIFAR10 certified-training IMP+NRSLoss improvement of $+8.2$ percentage points verified accuracy and $+8.1$ percentage points standard accuracy at $\epsilon=2/255$, adversarial-training verified-accuracy increases up to $+24.5$ percentage points on CIFAR10 for some pruning schemes, and comparable dataset-specific gains on FashionMNIST and SVHN (certified-training gains roughly $2.5\text{--}6.3\%$, adversarial-training verified gains roughly $21.0\text{--}41.5\%$) as reported in the authors' experimental tables and descriptions.

open_questions.content: The authors acknowledge multiple unresolved scientific issues and practical limitations remaining after this work: (1) scalability: all complete-verification experiments are limited to relatively small convolutional models that fit a single 24GB GPU; it remains unresolved how the pruning benefits (verified-accuracy gains, verification-time and memory reductions, and certified-lottery-ticket existence) scale to substantially larger architectures used in practice, because complete verification for larger networks triggers out-of-memory/time constraints; (2) optimal stability–expressiveness trade-off: pruning reduces neuron instability but also reduces network expressiveness (if too many neurons become stable the network approaches linearity and standard accuracy degrades). Designing principled methods to select sparsity levels or stability-regularization strengths that maximize verified accuracy without unacceptable standard-accuracy loss remains unresolved; (3) generality across verifiers and training regimes: while experiments cover auto-LiRPA and FGSM+GradAlign and a comparison to FastIBP is presented, a broader theoretical and empirical characterization of pruning's effects across other certified-training algorithms, other complete verifiers, different model families, and larger perturbation regimes is still open; (4) automated discovery and theoretical characterization of certified lottery tickets: the conditions under which a subnetwork can be a certified lottery ticket (existence proofs, bounds on sparsity vs. certification preservation, and efficient algorithms to find such tickets at scale) remain open; and (5) NRSLoss hyperparameterization and BN interactions: the choice to stop gradients into $\gamma$ and the empirical NRSLoss weight (0.01) were set empirically in this work—formal guidance, robustness to these hyperparameters, and potential alternative BN-aware stability regularizers that are theoretically justified are unresolved.
